title: Agent Guardrails and Human Approvals
description: Learn how to safely run agents with tools by defining clear boundaries, approval gates, and fallback behavior before deployment.

data.text: Agentic systems are powerful because they can act, not just answer. That power raises risk. A good agent setup starts with boundaries: what tools it can use, what actions require human approval, and what should happen when confidence is low.

data.caption: Use approval gates for medium/high-risk actions before execution.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
  A[User request] --> B[Agent plans steps]
  B --> C{Action risk level}
  C -->|Low| D[Execute automatically]
  C -->|Medium| E[Show preview + require click approval]
  C -->|High| F[Escalate to human reviewer]
  D --> G[Log action + result]
  E --> G
  F --> G
  G --> H[Return final response]

  style D fill:#d1f3d8,stroke:#1a7f37,color:#1a7f37
  style E fill:#fff8c5,stroke:#9a6700,color:#9a6700
  style F fill:#ffebe9,stroke:#cf222e,color:#cf222e

data.title: Minimum guardrails before launch
items: Tool allowlist (only approved tools can be called)
Scope constraints (which data sources and actions are allowed)
Audit logging for every tool call
Fallback behavior when confidence is low or tool fails

data.title: Guardrail principles
points: Autonomy should be proportional to risk
High-risk actions always need human approval
Clear tool boundaries prevent accidental misuse
Audit logs are essential for accountability and debugging
Safe defaults matter more than maximum autonomy

data.text: Guardrails should be calibrated to consequence. Overly strict approvals create bottlenecks, while weak controls increase incident risk. The goal is risk-proportionate friction.

cards.title: Permissive
cards.description: Agent can use any tool freely. Fast but risky — a single mistake can cause data loss or compliance violations.

cards.title: Moderate
cards.description: Agent needs approval for medium/high-risk actions. Good balance of speed and safety for most business use cases.

cards.title: Strict
cards.description: Every tool call requires human approval. Safest but slowest. Best for financial, legal, or medical contexts.

data.title: Real approval workflow example
data.content:
A customer support agent wants to issue a $200 refund.

Step 1: Agent detects refund request and checks order total.
Step 2: Policy rule says refunds under $500 require manager approval.
Step 3: Agent pauses and shows the manager: 'Customer requests $200 refund for order #1234. Approve?'
Step 4: Manager clicks Approve.
Step 5: Agent processes the refund and logs the action.

Without the approval gate, the agent might have issued the refund immediately — which is fine here, but the same pattern applied to a $5,000 refund would be dangerous.

data.title: Warning
data.text: Never deploy an agent that can write to production, send emails, or modify records without at least one human approval gate for high-risk actions. The cost of a single bad action far exceeds the convenience of full automation.

data.title: End-to-end approval workflow
data.content:
A marketing automation agent wants to schedule a LinkedIn post.

1. Agent drafts post and checks brand guidelines.
2. Policy says: external posts require team-lead approval.
3. Agent creates a preview card: 'Draft post for @company — approve to schedule?'
4. Team lead reviews, suggests one edit.
5. Agent applies edit and reposts preview.
6. Team lead clicks Approve.
7. Agent schedules post and logs: approved_by=team_lead, scheduled_at=timestamp.

This workflow is safe because the agent cannot post without approval, and every step is logged for audit.

data.title: Important
data.text: The best approval workflows feel like a conversation, not a bureaucracy. Show the user exactly what will happen, let them edit, and log the decision. This builds trust while keeping safety.
